appraisal_events.evidence: « je ne connaissais pas d'homme qui, sous le rapport de l'intelligence et de la sensibilité, fût aussi doué que Jupien »; « son simple sens inné, son goût naturel... lui avaient fait composer ce parler si juste où toutes les symétries du langage se laissaient découvrir et montraient leur beauté ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator makes an explicit, superlative personal judgment praising Jupien's natural intelligence and verbal sensibility, a distinct local movement independent of the Charlus diminishment already captured.

appraisal_events.evidence: « le métier qu'il faisait pouvait à bon droit passer, certes, pour un des plus lucratifs, mais pour le dernier de tous. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly ranks Jupien's occupation as the lowest of all trades despite its profitability, a clear local social diminishment distinct from his praised personal qualities.

appraisal_events.evidence: « tous les efforts que le fils du maître d'hôtel et le neveu de Françoise avaient faits pour s'embusquer, Saint-Loup les avait faits en sens inverse, et avec succès, pour être en plein danger »; « Il ne disait pas « Boches », il leur avait fait l'éloge de la bravoure des Allemands, il n'attribuait pas à la trahison que nous n'eussions pas été vainqueurs dès le premier jour. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator underscores Saint-Loup's genuine sought-out courage and his magnanimous refusal of chauvinistic rhetoric about the Germans, locally elevating him in moral and personal terms, even though the household staff fails to appreciate it.

status_effects.explanation: Jupien is strongly elevated by the narrator's explicit superlative admiration for his natural intelligence and eloquence.
His profession is branded the lowest of all trades despite its profitability, locally lowering his social standing.
The narrator endorses Saint-Loup's authentic bravery and moral generosity toward the enemy, elevating him despite the household staff's cool, unappreciative reception.

ambiguities: Françoise and the maître d'hôtel (the latter not a scorable candidate) form a 'médiocre impression' of Saint-Loup and remain 'froids' toward him, valuing chauvinistic bravado he refuses to display; this local coolness runs counter to the narrator's own elevation of Saint-Loup and was not scored as a separate event to keep the supplement conservative, but it nuances his local reception.

Mme Verdurin's reported wish/prediction that Charlus be poisoned ('selon les prédictions et les voeux de Mme Verdurin') shows continued hostility from her toward Charlus, but since Charlus is an already-scored character, this could not be captured as a scoreable event under the scope rules.
